title: How PROV Sources, Sells and Collects: Distribution & Unit Economics
web_title: 3. How PROV Sources, Sells and Collects: Distribution & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: How PROV Sources, Sells and Collects: Distribution & Unit Economics
question: How does a pouch of dry fruit get from an orchard to a shelf, and how much of each ₹100 of sales turns into cash?

epigraph.quote: “We recognise that sustainable growth requires financial discipline, operational excellence and the ability to convert earnings into healthy cash flows over time.”
epigraph.author: D. P. Jhawar, Managing Director & CEO, H1 FY27 shareholders’ letter, 13 November 2026

web_blocks.title: Sourcing: from California packers to a Mumbai warehouse

web_blocks.html: PROV starts as an importer. In FY2026 the standalone parent, Proventus Agrocom Ltd (PAL), paid ₹281 crore for imports in foreign currency and earned no foreign exchange [3]. That equals about 34% of consolidated cost of goods (₹833 crore) and, by our arithmetic, 53% of PAL's own ₹530 crore of stock purchases. The rest comes from Indian mandis and traders; the prospectus put local procurement at 40–50% of needs [10].

Named FY2026 origins are the USA, West Africa, Australia, Afghanistan, Chile, the Middle East and India [5]. The USA supplied 33.5% of imports in FY2022 and 61.2% in the first nine months of FY2023 [10]. The prospectus claims direct ties with 30+ California packers and showed the top ten suppliers at 36.2% of purchases [10]. Later supplier concentration is not disclosed.

Two policy levers sit on top. In mid-2025 India charged 100% duty on US walnuts and ₹100 a kilogram on almond kernels, and importers delayed clearance hoping for cuts of roughly 50% [52][53]. Whether a cut took effect by November 2026 is not verified, and PROV does not disclose landed cost. From September 2025 GST on nuts and makhana snacks fell from 12% to 5%, and PROV says 98% of its brand portfolio sits in the 5% slab [35][51]. Our reading is that this mainly lifts demand and eases shelf prices, not margin.

Price swings are the bigger test. After Diwali 2024 dry-fruit raw-material prices rose about 25%, and the CEO said passing costs on takes about one month [9]. During that month the P&L absorbs the hit. FY2025 EBITDA of ₹12.92 crore missed the ₹22 crore an analyst said had been guided [9]. No hedging policy is disclosed, and there were no open commodity futures at 31 March 2026 [3]. So protection comes from repricing speed, and ₹59.45 crore of stock sat unhedged that day [3].

web_blocks.title: Packing: one plant at about three-quarters load, a second just opened

web_blocks.html: Mumbai is where almonds, cashews and mixes become pouches. The Khairane plant packs 1.5 lakh pouches a day on 47,000 sq ft with 300+ workers [3]. H1 FY27 sales averaged about 1.13 lakh pouches a day (2.07 crore pouches over 183 days), roughly 75% of that figure [2]. The utilisation is our inference, and co-packer volume is undisclosed.

Surat shows how plans slip. In September 2024 the subsidiary bought a 180,000+ sq ft site for about ₹12 crore and promised operations by year-end [25]. In May 2025 the CEO said Surat should run by the end of FY2026 [9]. The 13 November 2026 letter reports Phase 1 complete with ₹14 crore of capex, and Phases 2 and 3 plus cold storage due by June 2027 [2]. That is roughly a year and a half late. Target capacity moved from 8 lakh units a day to 4 lakh, then 4 lakh+ and now 5 lakh+ [25][19][2]. An ICICI term loan helps fund it [3].

In Bihar the subsidiary runs a makhana unit at Purnia, called 2,500 tonnes a year and commenced on 12 May 2026 [8]. A July 2026 release says Bihar is being expanded towards that level over three years [7]. The statements conflict, so we treat current output as unproven. The deck claims 300+ bps of margin gain after commissioning [5], with no volume or yield figure behind it.

PAL's own accounts show a trader that sells most output to its subsidiary. Of ₹535 crore standalone revenue in FY2026, ₹324.67 crore (61%) went to Prov Foods Pvt Ltd (PFPL), against 70% in FY2025 [3]. PFPL, 98.75% owned, packs the goods and sells them as ProV. It reported turnover of ₹721.3 crore and PAT of ₹10.19 crore, about 71% of group PAT [3]. Adding the two companies and removing ₹324.7 crore gives ₹931.9 crore, ₹7 crore above group revenue, so other internal flows exist that we cannot itemise [3].

PAL's external sales, our estimate ₹210.6 crore, are mostly bulk and white-label. PAL also lent PFPL ₹29.86 crore of IPO money in 2023, and ₹14.86 crore was outstanding in March 2026 [3][24]. Shareholders approved related-party dealings up to ₹400 crore a year in September 2025, and the 2026 AGM notice sought up to ₹677.5 crore [3][33]. PAL's standalone EBITDA margin of 0.66% before other income therefore says little: the brand, the pouches and most credit risk sit in PFPL.

PROV sells through general trade, modern trade, e-commerce and quick commerce, plus bulk and white-label sales and a small online store [2][40]. The FY2024 deck's pie charts, whose labels extracted jumbled, imply general trade fell from about 73% of brand sales in FY2022 to 32% in FY2024 as modern trade and e-commerce each reached about a third [17]. Management still calls general trade the backbone [9]. The FY2026 split is not disclosed, except quick commerce at 5–7% with a goal above 10% [42][3].

web_blocks.caption: Sales route, channel, risk and evidence
rows: Distributors to 16,000+ touchpoints; field force 80+, 200+, 350+, then 600+ in 205+ cities [5][3][2]
Distributors were 45+ in FY2024; no later count [17]
D Mart, Reliance Retail, More, Metro C&C; promoters in 360 stores [10][3]
Top five customers were 38.0% of sales in 9M FY2023, no later data [10]
21.96% of brand revenue in FY2022; now not disclosed [10]
Mandi sales and packing for others; ₹177 crore, 28% of H1 FY27 [2]
web_blocks.takeaway: Channel margins, trade terms and customer concentration after FY2023 are not disclosed, so the mix cannot be converted into profit by channel.

web_blocks.html: The fastest-growing channels, modern trade and e-commerce, hand pricing and promotion power to a few large buyers. General trade keeps the buyer base wide but needs people and credit. PROV answered by multiplying its field force more than sevenfold in three years. Some of the 115% jump in H1 FY27 employee cost is contract staff moved onto payroll [2].

Management reports marketing investment of ₹14 crore in FY2024, ₹30 crore in FY2025 and ₹75 crore in FY2026 [3]. The audited expense note shows one line, Marketing, Advertising and Business Promotion, at ₹20.21 crore for FY2026 against ₹4.55 crore a year earlier [3]. The other ₹54.8 crore is not a named line. It is probably netted against revenue as trade schemes, or spread across packing, freight and warehousing lines, but the filings do not say.

This changes how you read margin. Management's 22.1% gross margin on ₹659 crore of brand revenue would be ₹145.6 crore, more than the whole group's audited gross profit of ₹91.6 crore [3][5]. They cannot be one measure. Our judgment is that the audited 9.9% is what the business keeps after trade spend and is the right base for unit economics. The 22.1% may be a fair brand KPI, but no audited line supports it.

web_blocks.title: A worked ₹100: FY2026 audited revenue to free cash flow

web_blocks.html: The waterfall follows ₹100 of FY2026 consolidated revenue to cash. Every input is audited for the year to 31 March 2026, with no half-year or trailing figures mixed in [3]. Materials and stock cost is cost of materials (₹648.15 crore) plus purchases of stock in trade (₹198.52 crore) less the ₹13.31 crore inventory build.

notes.revenue: Audited consolidated revenue from operations, year to 31 March 2026 [3].
notes.cogs: Cost of materials ₹648.15 Cr + purchases ₹198.52 Cr − inventory build ₹13.31 Cr = ₹833.37 Cr [3].
notes.employee_cost: Employee benefit expense; PAL itself has only 18 on-roll staff [3].
notes.other_opex: Other expenses, including packing, freight, warehousing and promotion lines [3].
notes.interest: Finance cost on ₹27.05 Cr of borrowings at March 2026 [3].
notes.other_income: Includes interest income; nil derivative trading result in FY2026 [3].
notes.tax: Current ₹2.22 Cr, deferred ₹1.36 Cr and earlier years ₹0.02 Cr [3].
notes.cfo: Audited cash flow from operations; operating cash before working capital was ₹19.48 Cr [3].
notes.capex: Includes capital advances; Surat was capitalised mainly in H1 FY27 [3][1].

web_blocks.caption: Audited consolidated FY2026 waterfall (₹ crore inputs, each row scaled deterministically to ₹100 of revenue)
web_blocks.takeaway: Of every ₹100 of FY2026 revenue, ₹90.10 went on nuts and packaging inputs and ₹7.91 on people and overheads. About ₹1.99 was EBITDA before other income and ₹1.54 was profit after tax. Only ₹0.98 arrived as operating cash and ₹0.74 as free cash flow.

web_blocks.html: Cash fell short of profit: CFO of ₹9.06 crore was 64% of PAT of ₹14.26 crore. Operating cash before working capital was ₹19.48 crore, and working capital took ₹8.65 crore and tax ₹1.77 crore [3]. Free cash flow of ₹6.81 crore is flattered by capex of only ₹2.24 crore, because Surat was mostly capitalised after year-end.

web_blocks.caption: Per ₹100 of revenue: FY2025, FY2026 and H1 FY27 (H1 unaudited, six months, not annualised)
web_blocks.takeaway: Sources [3][1]. H1 materials cost is derived from the 12.0% reported gross margin; H1 lines carry about ±₹1 lakh of reading error because the filing is a scanned image.

web_blocks.html: Profit per ₹100 rose from ₹1.27 to ₹1.54 to ₹1.87, because a falling materials share more than paid for higher overheads in H1 FY27 (other expenses 8.06 against 6.84). The cash row says the opposite. FY2025 and H1 FY27 absorbed far more than they earned, and only FY2026 was positive.

web_blocks.title: Working capital: the build in H1, the release in H2

web_blocks.html: PROV pays suppliers fast and collects slowly, so it funds its own growth. Screener-derived ratios give FY2026 payable days of about 10, debtor days of 15 and inventory days of 26, a cash cycle near 31 days [67]. Management quotes 61 days on its own definition [5]. Supplier advances of ₹19.05 crore almost cancel trade payables of ₹22.57 crore, so suppliers lend PROV little [3]; credit terms are undisclosed.

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital build, March 2026 versus September 2026 (consolidated, ₹ crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Balances are from the audited and limited-review balance sheets [3][1]; March net cash includes ₹21.14 crore of liquid funds, almost none left by September.

web_blocks.html: Receivables doubled while half-year revenue was 18% above H2 FY2026. On H1 revenue that is about 23 receivable days against 15 in March. Festive stocking and slower payment by large buyers both fit; the filings cannot separate them. H1 FY27 CFO was −₹57.64 crore, after −₹34.16 crore in H1 FY2026, and by our derivation H2 FY2026 released about ₹43 crore. The seasonal pattern is real but has one full year of evidence. FY2023 to FY2025 audited CFO was negative each year, and four-year CFO of ₹0.69 crore sits against ₹32.5 crore of PAT [15][3].

web_blocks.the_number: Our estimate is that PROV needs ₹12–15 of net working capital per ₹100 of annual revenue, so retained profit funds only about 10–16% of the working capital its growth requires.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Net working capital is receivables plus inventories plus short-term loans and advances less payables. At March 2026 it was ₹107.07 crore on FY2026 revenue of ₹924.99 crore, or 11.6%. At September 2026 it was ₹186.71 crore on annualised H1 revenue of ₹1,266.5 crore, or 14.7%. PAT per ₹100 (1.54 in FY2026, 1.87 in H1 FY27) divided by those intensities gives 1.54 ÷ 14.7 = 10.5% and 1.87 ÷ 11.6 = 16.1%.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Balances from the audited March 2026 and limited-review September 2026 balance sheets [3][1]. H1 revenue of ₹633.26 crore is doubled only to give a rough annual base, which ignores the stronger festive H2.
web_blocks.the_range: Intensity of 11.6% to 14.7%; self-funding share of about 10% to 16%. September is a seasonal high, so steady state probably sits nearer the lower intensity.
web_blocks.if_off: If Surat cold storage cuts inventory days, or H2 collections release more than in FY2026, intensity falls and growth funds itself faster. If large buyers keep stretching payment, intensity moves toward 15% and bank debt must keep rising with sales.

web_blocks.html: Banks fill the gap. ICICI Bank is the only lender named in the annual report. Its working-capital facility, secured on stock and book debts, costs 9.15%, and borrowings were ₹27.05 crore at March 2026 [3]. Sanctioned limits and letter-of-credit use are not disclosed, though PAL issued letters of comfort for PFPL's higher limits in October 2023 and October 2025 [41][30]. By September 2026 consolidated short-term borrowing was ₹46.73 crore and long-term ₹9.68 crore [1].

web_blocks.title: Profit first, cash later
paragraphs: PROV earns its rupee twice: once when goods are invoiced and again when retailers pay and stock turns. The first has been shown for four years, the second for one half-year cycle.

The evidence says PROV is a real distribution business with a thin margin and a heavy working-capital appetite. It does not yet show that growth can finance itself, that the 22% management margin survives trade spend, or that Bihar and Surat lower unit costs.

book_paragraphs: Let me walk you through a packet of cashews, because the whole business hides inside it. Start at the dock. Somewhere in California a packer shells and sorts almonds. PROV's parent company, Proventus Agrocom, pays for the container in dollars, roughly ₹281 crore of imports in FY2026, and earns not one dollar back. That is a one-way exposure to the exchange rate and to the price of the nut itself.

What protects the margin? Not a hedge book. Nothing is disclosed, and no commodity futures were open at March 2026. The protection is speed. When prices jumped about 25% after Diwali 2024, the CEO told analysts that, in his words, "it takes one month to pass on". Think about what that means. For about thirty days the company eats the increase. FY2025 EBITDA of ₹12.92 crore against a guided ₹22 crore is what thirty days of that looked like, together with a doubling of marketing.

Policy sits on top of price. In mid-2025 India charged 100% duty on US walnuts, and importers were holding shipments back hoping for cuts near 50%. I could not verify what finally happened, and PROV does not publish its landed cost, so I leave the duty question open. The GST cut from 12% to 5% in September 2025 is cleaner. It lowers the shelf price of almost the entire ProV range, which should help demand. I would not expect it to lift margin by itself.

Now follow the goods inside the group, because this is the part that surprises people. The parent buys the nuts. It sells ₹324.67 crore of them, 61% of its revenue, to its own subsidiary, Prov Foods. The subsidiary packs them at Khairane in Navi Mumbai and sells under the ProV label. Add the two companies together and you double count. The consolidated ₹925 crore is the honest number. Why should you care? Because the parent's 0.66% margin tells you nothing, while the subsidiary's ₹10.19 crore profit is about 71% of the group's.

Picture the Khairane floor in the second half of the year. About 300 workers, two shifts, a plant rated at 1.5 lakh pouches a day. In H1 FY27 it averaged about 1.13 lakh. That is roughly three-quarters, my inference and not a company statistic. Now picture the plant management promised in Surat. In September 2024 the plan was operations by year-end. In May 2025 the CEO said it "should be up and running by the end of Financial Year '26". In November 2026 Phase 1 was finally reported complete, with ₹14 crore of capex. A late plant is not a scandal. A pattern of late plants is information, and you should weigh the next date accordingly.

Then comes the makhana unit in Purnia. One press release says 2,500 tonnes are operating. Another, two months later, says the plant is being expanded towards 2,500 tonnes over three years. I cannot reconcile them and I will not pretend to. Until there is a volume figure, I treat the 300 bps margin gain promised from Bihar as a hope with a number attached.

After the pouch is packed, it must find a hand. PROV has four routes. General trade runs through distributors to roughly 16,000 outlets, and the field force has grown from 80 to over 600 people. Modern trade means D Mart, Reliance Retail and others, with promoters standing in 360 busy stores. Then come Amazon, Flipkart and BigBasket, and the quick-commerce apps, Blinkit and Zepto. The company will not tell you what share each channel carries today, and I would not guess. What I can say is that the fastest-growing routes put a few big buyers across the table from a company with a two-rupee margin. The FY2024 deck hints at the drift: general trade was about 73% of brand sales in FY2022 and about 32% two years later, though those charts are hard to read and I hold the figures loosely.

Here is a question to put to every brand-led company: where did the promotion money go? Management says it spent ₹75 crore on marketing in FY2026. The audited expense note shows a line of ₹20.21 crore. The remaining ₹55 crore or so is not visible as an expense, which suggests it is netted against sales as schemes and discounts. If so, reported revenue is already net of trade spend, and the 9.9% audited gross margin is the one that pays the bills. Management's 22.1% would imply ₹146 crore of gross profit, more than the whole group's audited ₹92 crore.

So take ₹100 of invoices and follow it. ₹90.10 buys nuts and packaging. People and everything else take ₹7.91. About ₹1.99 is left as operating profit, and ₹1.54 after tax. And cash? Only ₹0.98 came in as operating cash flow, and ₹0.74 as free cash flow once the small FY2026 capex is taken out. The gap is working capital. Suppliers are paid within about ten days, and ₹19 crore of advances sits with them. Customers take 15 days or more. Inventory sits for about 26.

Now the part I would underline twice. Between March and September 2026, receivables went from ₹38.69 crore to ₹78.56 crore. Inventories rose from ₹59.45 crore to ₹88.37 crore. Cash flow from operations was minus ₹57.64 crore for the half. A company with net cash of about ₹19.6 crore became one with net debt of about ₹51 crore in six months. Management calls this the build before the festive peak, and last year's second half released about ₹43 crore, so the argument is not empty. But it has one year of proof against three earlier years of negative operating cash.

My own rough arithmetic is that every ₹100 of annual revenue needs ₹12 to ₹15 of working capital. At a profit of ₹1.54 to ₹1.87 per ₹100, retained profit covers only a tenth to a sixth of that need. The rest is bank debt, and the only banker named is ICICI at about 9.15%. That is not alarming at today's size. It does mean growth of 60% a year is partly bought on credit, and the CEO's own letter concedes the point when it speaks of converting earnings into cash "over time".

So what has the evidence settled, and what has it left open? It has settled that PROV buys directly, packs competently, reaches a very wide set of shops and platforms, and earns a small but rising profit on every rupee it invoices. It has not settled whether that profit turns into cash without the bank, whether the second plant lifts margins or merely adds fixed cost, or whether the brand can hold its price when a rival pushes a 25% input swing back onto shoppers. Those three questions decide the next chapters.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A brand is only half a business model. The other half is the unglamorous loop of paying for nuts, packing them, getting retailers to pay and doing it again. PROV has shown it can make that loop spin faster each year. What it has not yet shown is that the loop pays for itself. Keep two clocks in view: the one that records profit when you invoice, and the one that records cash when you are paid.
